summary: Defines a method for negotiating data encryption over PPP links. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: ECP is the control protocol that lets two ends of a PPP link turn on encryption between them. It works much like the protocol that sets up the link in the first place: one end offers the ciphers it can handle, the other end picks one, and encrypted data may then flow. The RFC also defines how the two ends recover when a packet cannot be decrypted.

questions: what is the ppp encryption control protocol
what ppp protocol value is used for encrypted datagrams
how does ppp negotiate which cipher to use
subtitle: How the two ends of a PPP link agree to encrypt their traffic, and which cipher to use.

tldr.problem: A PPP link carries traffic between two peers, and the peers often need that traffic to be encrypted, but they first have to agree on an algorithm before any data can flow.
tldr.mechanism: ECP is the Link Control Protocol repeated with encryption options: after the link is up, the end that can decrypt offers one or more algorithms, and the other end accepts one, rejects the rest, or asks for corrected values, and only then may encrypted datagrams be sent.
tldr.outcome: The negotiation settles on a single algorithm per direction, and the memo defines a Reset-Request and Reset-Ack pair so that a decryption failure in one direction does not tear down the traffic in the other.

today:
RFC 1968 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that defines the PPP Encryption Control Protocol.

The memo says that at the time of writing only DESE, the PPP DES Encryption Protocol, was registered as a publicly available encryption type, and it points to the Assigned Numbers RFC for later additions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol (PPP) provides a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links, and it defines an extensible Link Control Protocol (LCP). To establish communications over a PPP link, each end of the link must first send LCP packets to configure and test the data link during the Link Establishment phase. After the link has been established, optional facilities may be negotiated as needed.

One such facility is data encryption. A wide variety of encryption methods may be negotiated, although typically only one method is used in each direction of the link. A different encryption algorithm may be negotiated in each direction, for speed, cost, memory or other considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP links are set up in stages. First the two ends configure and test the link itself. After that they can agree on extras, and one of those extras is encryption. The two directions may end up using different ciphers, for instance because one direction is slower and cheaper to encrypt.

sections.title: The Encryption Control Protocol
sections.content:
The Encryption Control Protocol (ECP) is responsible for configuring and enabling data encryption algorithms on both ends of the point-to-point link. It uses the same packet exchange mechanism as LCP, and ECP packets may not be exchanged until PPP has reached the Network-Layer Protocol phase; ECP packets received before that phase is reached should be silently discarded.

ECP is exactly the same as LCP with a few exceptions. Its packets may use any modifications to the basic frame format that were negotiated during the Link Establishment phase. Exactly one ECP packet is encapsulated in the PPP Information field, where the PPP Protocol field indicates type hex 8053 for the Encryption Control Protocol. When individual link data encryption is used in a multiple link connection to a single destination, the PPP Protocol field indicates type hex 8055 for the Individual link Encryption Control Protocol. ECP also has its own distinct set of Configuration Options.

On negotiation, an implementation must not transmit data until ECP negotiation has completed successfully, and if the ECP negotiation is not successful the link should be brought down. An implementation should also be prepared to wait for Authentication and Link Quality Determination to finish before timing out waiting for a Configure-Ack or another response.
sections.plainLanguage: ECP reuses the link setup protocol, with encryption added. It runs only once the link is already carrying network traffic, and it is marked in the packet header by a special protocol number so the two ends know the packets belong to it. No data may be sent until the negotiation has succeeded, and a failed negotiation should close the link.

sections.title: Sending Encrypted Datagrams
sections.content:
Before any encrypted packets may be communicated, PPP must reach the Network-Layer Protocol phase and ECP must reach the Opened state. An encrypted packet is encapsulated in the PPP Information field, where the PPP Protocol field indicates type hex 0053, encrypted datagram.

When multiple PPP links lead to a single destination there are two ways to use encryption. The first encrypts the data before sending it out through the multiple links, and the PPP Protocol field must indicate type hex 0053. The second treats each link as a separate connection that may or may not have encryption enabled, and on links that have negotiated encryption the PPP Protocol field must be type hex 0055, individual link encrypted datagram.

Only one encryption algorithm is in use in each direction at a time, and it is negotiated before the first encrypted frame is sent. The PPP Protocol field of the encrypted datagram says that the frame is encrypted, but not which algorithm was used.

The maximum length of an encrypted packet transmitted over a PPP link is the same as the maximum length of the Information field of a PPP encapsulated packet. If the encryption algorithm is likely to make the message longer than that, multilink should also be negotiated to allow fragmentation of the frames, even if only a single link is used. If the encryption algorithm carries history between frames, the algorithm must supply a way of determining whether it is passing data reliably, or it must require the use of a reliable transport such as LAPB.

Compression may also be negotiated with the Compression Control Protocol. To ensure interoperability, plain text must be compressed first and then encrypted. That order was chosen because it should give smaller output and more secure encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the negotiation has finished, encrypted frames go out in the same place as ordinary PPP frames, with a protocol number that says the contents are encrypted. If the cipher makes frames longer than the link can take, the two ends must also agree to split them up. When compression is used as well, the data is compressed first and encrypted second.

sections.title: Reset-Request and Reset-Ack
sections.content:
ECP includes Reset-Request and Reset-Ack codes so that a decryption failure in one direction of the link can be signalled without affecting traffic in the other direction. Some encryption algorithms may not need this mechanism, and each algorithm has to specify how a decryption failure is detected. On the initial detection of a failure, an ECP implementation should transmit an ECP packet with the Code field set to 14, Reset-Request; the Data field may be filled with any desired data. Once a Reset-Request has been sent, any encrypted packets received are discarded, and further Reset-Requests may be sent with the same Identifier until a valid Reset-Ack is received.

When the link is busy, one decryption error is usually followed by several more before the Reset-Ack can be received. It is undesirable to transmit Reset-Requests more frequently than the round-trip time of the link, because that results in redundant Reset-Requests and Reset-Acks being transmitted and processed. The receiver may limit transmission of Reset-Requests, to say one per second, while a Reset-Ack is outstanding.

On reception of a Reset-Request, the transmitting encrypter is reset to an initial state, and an ECP packet must be transmitted with the Code field set to 15, Reset-Ack, the Identifier field copied from the Reset-Request packet, and the Data field filled with any desired data. On receipt of a Reset-Ack, the receiving decrypter is reset to an initial state. Since several Reset-Acks may be in the pipe, the decrypter must be reset for each Reset-Ack that matches the currently expected identifier.

The packet format is the one LCP defines: a Code field, an Identifier field, a Length field and a Data field. The Identifier must change whenever the content of the Data field changes and whenever a valid reply has been received for a previous request, but it should stay unchanged for retransmissions. The Data field is zero or more octets of uninterpreted data for the sender's use, of any length from zero to the peer's established MRU minus four.
sections.plainLanguage: If a frame cannot be decrypted, the two ends need to start the cipher again from a known point, in one direction only. The end that noticed the problem sends a Reset-Request; the other end puts its sending side back to its starting state and answers with a Reset-Ack. Frames that arrive in between are thrown away, and the request is repeated until the answer comes back.

sections.title: ECP Configuration Options
sections.content:
ECP Configuration Options allow encryption algorithms and their parameters to be negotiated. ECP uses the same Configuration Option format LCP defines, with a separate set of options. An option indicates an algorithm that the receiver is willing or able to use to decrypt data sent by the sender, so a system may offer to accept several algorithms and negotiate a single one that will be used.

Two option types are defined. Option 0 is the OUI, which provides a way to negotiate a proprietary encryption protocol. It distinguishes one vendor's protocol from another's by means of the Organisationally Unique Identifier (OUI), namely the first three octets of the vendor's Ethernet address assigned by IEEE 802. Since the first matching encryption will be used, the document recommends that any known OUI encryption options be transmitted first, before the common options. Before accepting the option, the implementation must verify that the OUI identifies a proprietary algorithm it can decrypt and that any vendor specific negotiation values are fully understood.

Option 1 is the publicly available encryption type, whose format is a Type field, a Length field and a Values field. The Type field carries a value from 1 to 254 indicating the encryption protocol option being negotiated, and DESE, the PPP DES Encryption Protocol, is option type 1. Vendors who want to use proprietary encryption may use the OUI mechanism instead of asking the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority for an assigned option number. All compliant ECP implementations should implement option 1, DESE, and at the time of writing only DESE is registered.
sections.plainLanguage: The options are how the two ends name the ciphers they understand. There is one option for ciphers defined in public standards and one for a vendor's own cipher, which is identified by the first three bytes of the vendor's hardware address. At the time of writing, the only publicly registered cipher was DESE, the PPP DES Encryption Protocol.

sections.title: Negotiating an Encryption Algorithm
sections.content:
ECP uses LCP option negotiation techniques to negotiate encryption algorithms. In contrast with most other LCP or NCP negotiation of multiple options, ECP negotiation is expected to converge on a single mutually agreeable option, one encryption algorithm, or on none. Encryption should be negotiated in both directions, but the algorithms may be different.

The end that is willing to decrypt using a particular encryption algorithm is called the Decrypter, and its peer is the Encrypter. A Decrypter supporting more than one algorithm may send a Configure-Request containing either an ordered list of options with the most-preferred algorithm first, or just its preferred option that has not already been rejected.

An Encrypter wishing to accept the first of several options may Configure-Ack all the options, which indicates complete acceptance of the first-listed, preferred, algorithm. If the Encrypter does not recognise an option, or is unwilling to support it, it must send a Configure-Reject for that option, and where more than one option is offered it should Configure-Reject all but a single preferred option. If the Encrypter Configure-Rejects all the offered ECP options and the Decrypter has no further options it can offer, the Encrypter should take the link down.

If the Encrypter recognises an option but cannot accept it because of the values in the request, or because of optional parameters missing from the request, it must send a Configure-Nak with the option modified appropriately. The Configure-Nak must contain only those options that would be acceptable, and the Decrypter should send a new Configure-Request with only the single preferred option, adjusted as the Configure-Nak specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: One end offers the ciphers it can handle, most preferred first. The other end either accepts the first one, refuses the ones it does not want, or asks for different settings within one it recognises. The exchange ends with both ends on the same cipher, or with the link being closed. The two ends may end up on different ciphers in each direction.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Negotiating encryption using PPP is designed to provide protection against eavesdropping on that link. The strength of the protection is dependent on the encryption algorithm used and on the care with which any secret used by the algorithm is protected.

The document is explicit that complete security can only be obtained through end-to-end security between hosts. Encrypting the link protects the traffic between the two ends of the link; it does not protect the traffic once it has left the link.
sections.plainLanguage: Encrypting a link protects what travels over it, but only for as long as the traffic stays on that link. The document says plainly that real end-to-end protection has to come from securing the connection between the two hosts themselves.

items.label: Configure-Request
items.desc: A decrypter offers the encryption algorithms it is willing to use.

items.label: Configure-Ack
items.desc: The encrypter accepts the option; it may ack all options to select the first listed.

items.label: Configure-Nak
items.desc: The option is recognised but its values are not acceptable.

items.label: Configure-Reject
items.desc: The option is not recognised, or the encrypter is unwilling to support it.

items.label: Terminate-Request
items.desc: An LCP code, reused by ECP.

items.label: Terminate-Ack
items.desc: An LCP code, reused by ECP.

items.label: Code-Reject
items.desc: An LCP code, reused by ECP; other unrecognised codes are answered with it.

items.label: Reset-Request
items.desc: Reports a decryption failure in one direction of the link.

items.label: Reset-Ack
items.desc: Answers a Reset-Request and resets the sending encrypter.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Copied from the Reset-Request into the Reset-Ack; unchanged for retransmissions.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length field of the packet, followed by the Data field.

fields.name: IEEE OUI
fields.desc: The first three octets of the vendor's Ethernet address.

fields.name: Subtype
fields.desc: Specific to each OUI; there is no standardisation for this field.
